extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners and patent practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating written description, new matter, and enablement under 35 U.S.C. 112 (and related statutes) in U.S. patent applications and patents, including examiner procedures, legal tests, and key case-law considerations. Covers range/subgenus support, rephrasing, inherency, incorporation by reference, Wands factors, working/prophetic examples, and examiner actions on new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written description requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe the claimed invention such that one skilled in the art reasonably understands that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter at the time of filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases show that reciting an undisclosed species may violate the description requirement (e.g., Ex parte Ohshiro). Whether subgeneric terminology is acceptable depends on what is reasonably communicated to those skilled in the art (cases: In re Lukach, Ex parte Sorenson, In re Smith, In re Wilder). Each case must be decided on its own facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Range limitations and numeric/subgenus support
rubrics_metrics.description: When claims recite numerical ranges or subgenus limitations, the analysis must determine which ranges or subgeneric members a person of ordinary skill would consider inherently supported by the original disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Wertheim — original disclosure of 25%-60% with examples of 36% and 50% did not support a new claim 'at least 35%' (because no upper limit), but 'between 35% and 60%' was acceptable. Case citations (Purdue Pharma, General Hosp. Corp., Union Oil) illustrate that overlap, discrete values, and whether the disclosure shows the inventors considered the claimed ratio as part of the invention are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship of written description to new matter (prohibition under 35 U.S.C. 132 and 251)
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment that adds content not described in the application as filed raises a new matter issue; 35 U.S.C. 132 prohibits introducing new matter in prosecution amendments and 35 U.S.C. 251 prohibits introducing new matter in reissue applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information from any part of the original application may be added to another part without introducing new matter, but adding content not originally disclosed is prohibited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of new matter — examiner actions
rubrics_metrics.description: If new subject matter is added to the disclosure, the examiner should object (under 35 U.S.C. 132 or 251) and require cancellation of the new matter; if new matter is added to the claims, the examiner should reject the claims under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (or pre-AIA 112, first paragraph) for lack of written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the specification is amended to add new matter that affects claim limitations, a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) should be made. The examiner should still consider the added subject matter for prior-art rejections even though a new matter rejection may be overcome by applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review of new matter objections and/or rejections (appealability)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an objection is 'determinative of the rejection' (e.g., examiner indicates disclosure contains new matter), the matter may be addressed by the Patent Trial and Appeal Board; if both a rejection and objection have been made, the issue becomes appealable and should not be decided by petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 1201 for procedures; ordinarily objections are petitionable and rejections are appealable, but determinative new matter objections move the issue to appeal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing permitted where supported
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments that merely rephrase a passage without changing its meaning do not constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere inclusion of dictionary or art-recognized definitions known at filing may not be new matter. If multiple definitions exist and an applicant adds a specific definition, the original application must make clear the intended definition to avoid new matter/written description issues (cases: In re Anderson; Schering Corp. v. Amgen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obvious error corrections
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to correct an obvious error do not constitute new matter where a person skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, applicant may not rely on a foreign priority document of record to support correction of an error in the pending U.S. application unless the U.S. application explicitly incorporates the foreign document by reference; special rules (37 CFR 1.55/1.57) address inadvertent omissions for certain filings after Sept. 21, 2004.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claimed subject matter disclosed only in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims as filed are part of the disclosure; if an original claim discloses material not found in the remainder of the specification, the specification may be amended to include that claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.44 where originally claimed subject matter lacks proper antecedent basis in the specification. This is an objection to the specification; enablement issues should be treated separately (see MPEP § 608.01(o) and § 2163.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent function, theory, or advantage (inherency doctrine)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the specification discloses an invention that inherently performs a function or has a property, the application necessarily discloses that function/property even if not explicitly stated, and the application may later be amended to recite it without introducing new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must show the missing descriptive matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be established by probabilities or possibilities (cases: In re Reynolds; Yeda Research; In re Robertson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An application may incorporate content of another document by reference; the incorporated information is treated as part of the application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replacing the identified incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter. See 37 CFR 1.57 and MPEP § 608.01(p) for Office policy and see MPEP § 2181 for impacts when 35 U.S.C. 112(f) / pre-AIA 112 sixth paragraph is invoked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (35 U.S.C. 112(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must describe how to make and how to use the invention so that one skilled in the art can make and use the invention as defined by the claims; the enablement requirement is separate from the written description requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to enable a perfected or commercially viable embodiment. The purpose is to communicate the invention to the interested public in a meaningful way. A claim is invalid if not supported by an enabling disclosure (cases: Vas-Cath v. Mahurkar; CFMT v. Yieldup).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of enablement — undue/unreasonable experimentation standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Enablement is assessed by whether one skilled in the art could make and use the invention from the disclosure and knowledge in the art without undue experimentation (Minerals Separation v. Hyde standard, and In re Wands framework).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determining enablement is a question of law based on underlying factual findings. Courts emphasize whether experimentation required would be 'undue' or 'unreasonable' (see Telectronics, In re Wands, and recent Supreme Court clarification in Amgen v. Sanofi).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantity of experimentation — reasonableness
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may require a reasonable amount of experimentation; what is 'reasonable' depends on the invention and the underlying art. Complex experimentation typical of the field may still be reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The test is not whether any experimentation is needed but whether the required experimentation is undue. See cases: In re Certain Limited-Charge Cell Culture Microcarriers; In re Wands; In re Angstadt. See MPEP § 2164.06 for further discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undue experimentation factors (Wands factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Wands factors to assess whether the amount of experimentation required is undue: (A) breadth of the claims; (B) nature of the invention; (C) state of the prior art; (D) level of skill in the art; (E) predictability in the art; (F) amount of direction provided by the inventor; (G) existence of working examples; (H) quantity of experimentation needed based on disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These factors are probative and must be weighed together — it is improper to conclude non-enablement based on analysis of only one factor. See cross-referenced MPEP sections for detailed discussion (e.g., § 2164.08, § 2164.05, § 2164.03, § 2164.02, § 2164.06).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to make the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification must disclose at least one method for making and using the claimed invention that bears a reasonable correlation to the entire scope of the claim; disclosing one method that correlates reasonably to claim scope may satisfy enablement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose other methods does not render a claim invalid if the one disclosed method is sufficient (cases: In re Fisher; Spectra-Physics). For inventions requiring particular apparatus or starting materials not readily available, the application must provide sufficient disclosure of those materials or apparatus (In re Ghiron; In re Howarth).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to use the claimed invention
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statement of utility in the specification implies how to use the invention, and standard modes of administration are known in the art, enablement is satisfied; dosage/method specifics need not be recited if they can be obtained without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim is limited by a particular use, enablement must be evaluated with respect to that use (In re Vaeck). If multiple uses are disclosed, enablement must support each disclosed use or explain why any enabled use correlates with the claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Working and prophetic examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples in the specification may be 'working' (based on actual work) or 'prophetic' (based on predicted results); enablement does not turn on having working examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prophetic examples should be drafted in present or future tense to distinguish them from working examples. Lack of working examples is a factor especially in unpredictable arts, but presence of prophetic examples alone should not be the basis for asserting non-enablement. Applicant need not have actually reduced the invention to practice prior to filing (cases: Gould v. Quigg; In re Chilowsky; In re Borkowski).

rubrics_metrics.name: None or one working example — sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A single working example in the specification can be sufficient to preclude a rejection that nothing is enabled, though rejections limiting enablement to particular scope may still be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If other factors point toward enablement, absence of working examples alone will not render the invention non-enabled. However, an absence of working examples can be relevant when assessing whether the specification enables the full scope of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments supported in the original description are not new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments to an application which are supported in the original description do not constitute new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere rephrasing is permissible; adding a definition requires that the original disclosure support that particular definition. Examples and precedent (In re Anderson, Schering) illustrate boundaries.
